seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 141 HTS Chapter 27 lines — crude oil, gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LNG, propane, coal, petroleum coke and electricity. Base rates from Free to 84¢ per barrel, Canadian oil Free under USMCA, energy exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, China 25%, and the Russian oil ban.

overview.intro:
Chapter 27 covers mineral fuels: coal, lignite and coke (2701–2704), coal-tar chemicals such as benzene and toluene (2707), **crude oil** (2709), **refined products** such as gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and lubricating oils (2710), **natural gas, LNG and propane** (2711), waxes, petroleum coke and bitumen (2712–2715) and **electricity** (2716). It is the largest U.S. import chapter by value: **$216.4B** in 2025, $146.8B of it crude oil and 55% from Canada.

The base tariffs are small and specific: Free on coal, natural gas, LNG and electricity; **5.25¢ or 10.5¢ per barrel** on crude oil; **52.5¢ per barrel** on gasoline and jet fuel; 84¢ per barrel on lubricating oils. Canadian and Mexican oil is **Free under USMCA**. Energy was exempted from nearly every 2025–2026 extra duty — the reciprocal tariff, the Section 122 surcharge and the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** (U.S. note 52(b)) — and the 2025 IEEPA duties, including **10% on non-USMCA Canadian energy**, ended on February 24, 2026. What still applies: **China's Section 301 duty** (25% on most lines), **Column 2 rates for Russia**, and sanctions that **ban Russian and Iranian oil**. Federal excise taxes on imported petroleum are owed on top and are not in the rate table.

productGroups.label: Coal and coal briquettes
productGroups.blurb: Anthracite, bituminous coal (including coking and thermal coal), other coal and coal briquettes: 6 lines, all Free. China pays 25% (List 3). Russian-origin coal is banned under Executive Order 14066.

productGroups.label: Lignite
productGroups.blurb: Lignite (brown coal), loose or agglomerated: 2 lines, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Peat
productGroups.blurb: Peat and peat litter, including horticultural peat moss: 1 line, Free. China pays 25% (List 3); Russia pays 35% in place of its Column 2 rate.

productGroups.label: Coke and semicoke
productGroups.blurb: Coke and semicoke of coal, lignite or peat, and retort carbon (metallurgical and foundry coke): 3 lines, Free. Coke is on none of the China Section 301 lists, so it is Free from China too.

productGroups.label: Coal gas and similar gases
productGroups.blurb: Coal gas, water gas, producer gas and similar manufactured gases (not natural gas): 1 line, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Coal tar and mineral tars
productGroups.blurb: Tar distilled from coal, lignite or peat and other mineral tars: 1 line, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Coal-tar distillation products (benzene, toluene, xylenes)
productGroups.blurb: Benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene, creosote oils, phenols and other products of high-temperature coal tar: 17 lines. Most are Free; carbazole and cresols pay 0.9¢/kg + 3% and phenol 2.9¢/kg + 12.5%.

productGroups.label: Pitch and pitch coke
productGroups.blurb: Pitch and pitch coke from coal tar or other mineral tars (binder pitch for aluminum anodes and electrodes): 2 lines, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Crude oil
productGroups.blurb: Crude petroleum and lease condensate: 5.25¢ per barrel below 25° API (heavy crude) and 10.5¢ per barrel at 25° API or more. Free under USMCA and most FTAs. China pays 25% on top; Russian and Iranian crude is banned.

productGroups.label: Refined petroleum products (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel)
productGroups.blurb: Gasoline, jet fuel, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, heating oil, residual fuel oil, lubricating oils, greases, biodiesel blends and waste oils: 76 lines, all dutiable — 52.5¢/bbl for motor fuel and jet fuel, 5.25–10.5¢/bbl for fuel oils, 84¢/bbl for lubricating oils, 7% for other oils.

productGroups.label: Natural gas, LNG and LPG (propane, butane)
productGroups.blurb: Liquefied natural gas, propane, butanes, ethylene, propylene and natural gas by pipeline: 17 lines, all Free. China pays 25% (List 3). Russian-origin LNG is banned; imports of natural gas need DOE authorization.

productGroups.label: Petroleum jelly and waxes
productGroups.blurb: Petroleum jelly, paraffin wax, microcrystalline wax, slack wax, montan wax and similar mineral waxes: 4 lines, Free. China pays 25% (paraffin wax 7.5%).

productGroups.label: Petroleum coke and bitumen
productGroups.blurb: Petroleum coke (calcined and not calcined), petroleum bitumen (asphalt binder) and other petroleum residues: 4 lines, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Natural bitumen, oil shale and tar sands
productGroups.blurb: Natural bitumen and asphalt, asphaltites and asphaltic rocks, bituminous or oil shale and tar sands: 2 lines, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Bituminous mixtures
productGroups.blurb: Bituminous mixtures based on natural asphalt, bitumen, petroleum bitumen, mineral tar or pitch (asphalt mastics, cut-backs): 1 line, Free. China pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Electricity
productGroups.blurb: Electrical energy: 1 line, Free from every country, including China (no Section 301 list covers it). Entered periodically rather than shipment by shipment (Additional U.S. note 6).

workedExamples.title: 500,000 barrels of heavy Canadian crude
workedExamples.body: Crude oil testing under 25° API pays **5.25¢ per barrel**. Claimed under USMCA (SPI S), it is **Free**; without a claim it is $26,250 (500,000 × $0.0525). U.S. note 52(b) exempts crude from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada, so nothing else is added. In 2025 a non-USMCA cargo also paid the 10% IEEPA energy duty until February 24, 2026. Not a tariff, but still owed: the **petroleum Superfund excise tax** on imported crude (16.4¢ per barrel in the statute, indexed for inflation ($0.18 per barrel for 2026)), paid to the IRS rather than CBP.

workedExamples.title: 300,000 barrels of gasoline from the Netherlands
workedExamples.body: Unleaded gasoline (motor fuel) pays **52.5¢ per barrel**: $157,500 on 300,000 barrels. The EU has no free trade agreement with the U.S., and the 10% Section 301 duty on EU goods does not apply because 2710.12.15 is on the note 52(b) exemption list. The importer must also meet EPA's fuel standards as a gasoline importer (40 CFR part 1090), carry renewable fuel obligations (40 CFR part 80), and pay federal excise tax of 18.4¢ per gallon when the gasoline is entered or removed at the terminal rack — none of which is in the tariff grid.

workedExamples.title: Lubricating oil from China
workedExamples.body: Engine lubricating oil pays **84¢ per barrel**, and because 2710.19.30 is on Section 301 **List 2**, Chinese-origin oil adds **25% of value** (9903.88.02). A $200,000 shipment of 1,000 barrels pays $840 + $50,000 = **$50,840**. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China does not stack on top (note 52(b)).

workedExamples.title: Crude oil or LNG from Russia
workedExamples.body: Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum fuels and products, LNG and coal **cannot be imported** into the United States: Executive Order 14066 has banned them since March 2022, and the national emergency behind it was continued on March 24, 2026. The tariff calculator does not model this ban; it would show Russia's Column 2 rate (21¢ per barrel). OFAC's guidance excludes Russian goods that were substantially transformed into a foreign-made product from "Russian Federation origin" (FAQ 1019).

**Note 2.** References in heading 2710 to "petroleum oils and oils obtained from bituminous minerals" include not only petroleum oils and oils obtained from bituminous minerals, but also similar oils, as well as those consisting mainly of mixed unsaturated hydrocarbons, obtained by any process, provided that the weight of the nonaromatic constituents exceeds that of the aromatic constituents. However, the references do not include liquid synthetic polyolefins of which less than 60 percent by volume distills at 300 °C, after conversion to 1,013 millibars when a reduced-pressure distillation method is used (chapter 39).

**Note 3.** For the purposes of heading 2710, "waste oils" means waste containing mainly petroleum oils and oils obtained from bituminous minerals (as described in note 2), whether or not mixed with water. These include: (a) such oils no longer fit for use as primary products (for example, used lubricating oils, used hydraulic oils and used transformer oils); (b) sludge oils from the storage tanks of petroleum oils, mainly containing such oils and a high concentration of additives (for example, chemicals) used in the manufacture of the primary products; and (c) such oils in the form of emulsions in water or mixtures with water, such as those resulting from oil spills, storage tank washings, or from the use of cutting oils for machining operations.

**Subheading notes.** (1) "Anthracite" (2701.11) is coal with a volatile matter limit (dry, mineral-matter-free basis) not exceeding 14%. (2) "Bituminous coal" (2701.12) has a volatile matter limit exceeding 14% and a calorific value of at least 5,833 kcal/kg (moist, mineral-matter-free basis). (3) In 2707.10–2707.40, benzol, toluol, xylol and naphthalene mean products with more than 50% by weight of benzene, toluene, xylenes or naphthalene. (4) In 2710.12, "light oils and preparations" are those of which 90% or more by volume (including losses) distill at 210 °C (ISO 3405 / ASTM D 86). (5) In heading 2710, "biodiesel" means mono-alkyl esters of fatty acids of a kind used as a fuel, derived from animal, vegetable or microbial fats and oils, whether or not used.

**Note 2.** For heading 2710, "petroleum oils" includes only products having a congealing point (ASTM D 938) below 30 °C or, if not below 30 °C, meeting the density and cone/needle penetration limits set out in the note.

**Note 3.** For 2710.12.15, "motor fuel" is any product derived primarily from petroleum, shale or natural gas, whether or not containing additives, which is principally used as a fuel in internal-combustion or other engines.

**Note 4.** For 2710.12.18, 2710.19.25 and 2710.20.15, "motor fuel blending stock" means any product (except naphthas of 2710.12.25) derived primarily from petroleum, shale oil or natural gas, whether or not containing additives, to be used for direct blending in the manufacture of motor fuel.

**Note 5.** In weighing the components of the mixtures of 2710.12.45 and 2710.19.45, naphtha and other petroleum derivatives present as solvents are disregarded.

**Note 6.** For heading 2716, "electrical energy" does not include electrical energy transmitted as a medium of communication, and electrical energy is not subject to the entry requirements of 19 U.S.C. 1484 but is entered on a periodic basis under Treasury regulations.

**Note 7.** A barrel (bbl) means 158.98 liters measured at 15.6 °C.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 27: Mineral Fuels & Oils — Oil & Gas Tariff Updates

seo.title: Oil & Gas Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Canadian Oil, Energy Exemptions, Russia & Venezuela (HTS Ch. 27) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. tariff change for crude oil, gasoline, diesel, natural gas, LNG and coal since January 2025: the 10% tariff on Canadian energy and when it ended, the energy exemptions from the reciprocal, Section 122 and 2026 Section 301 tariffs, China's Section 301 duties, and the Russia, Iran and Venezuela oil sanctions, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 141 Chapter 27 lines carry the same base rates in both — from Free on coal, natural gas and LNG to 5.25–10.5¢ per barrel on crude oil and 52.5¢ per barrel on gasoline and jet fuel.

What changed were the extra duties, and energy was carved out of most of them. In 2025 non-USMCA energy from **Canada** paid a **10%** IEEPA duty (other Canadian goods 25%, later 35%), non-USMCA goods from **Mexico** paid **25%**, and goods from **China** paid a 10–20% fentanyl duty. Every Chapter 27 subheading was on the exemption lists of the April 2025 reciprocal tariff, the Brazil and India IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 122 surcharge and the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** on 60 economies (U.S. note 52(b)). All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**.

Today the only extra tariffs are China's **Section 301** duties (25% on most lines, 7.5% on a few) and, for **Russia**, Column 2 rates — but Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum products, LNG and coal are **banned** outright under Executive Order 14066. Iranian-origin oil is banned under the Iran sanctions regulations, and Venezuelan oil can be bought only under a Treasury general license. Sanctions and federal excise taxes (the petroleum Superfund tax on crude and petroleum products) are listed below for reference; the tariff calculator does not price them.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 27 from any country (China Section 301 Lists 2, 3 and 4A; Russia's Column 2 and in-lieu rates; the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil actions, whose exemption lists cover the whole chapter; the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties), plus the sanctions-based import bans on Russian, Iranian and Venezuelan energy and the federal petroleum excise taxes, which the tariff calculator does not model. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 27 product. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: List 3 (+25%, 9903.88.03) covers 59 of the 76 Chapter 27 subheadings — coal, lignite, peat, coal tar and its products, crude oil, gasoline, jet fuel, diesel and fuel oils, natural gas, LNG, propane, petroleum jelly, petroleum coke, bitumen and asphalt. List 2 (+25%, 9903.88.02) covers lubricating oils and greases (2710.19.30–2710.19.40), and List 4A (+7.5%, 9903.88.15) phenol (2707.99.51), waste oils (2710.91, 2710.99) and paraffin wax (2712.20). Coke (2704) and electricity (2716) are on no list. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on China (9903.05.31) does not apply, because every Chapter 27 subheading is on the note 52(b) exemption list (9903.05.86). The IEEPA fentanyl duty on China ended February 24, 2026. USTR confirmed on October 7, 2026 that the 2018 actions continue during their four-year review.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Chinese-origin fuel, coal, LNG or wax pays 25% of its value on top of the base rate (7.5% for phenol, waste oil and paraffin wax). A $1 million cargo of Chinese gasoline pays $250,000 plus 52.5¢ per barrel. Chinese coke and electricity pay nothing extra.

inEffect.measure: Column 2 rates, 35% in lieu of Column 2 (peat) and Section 232 aluminum derivatives (one line)
inEffect.exemption: Russia has paid Column 2 rates since April 9, 2022 (Pub. L. 117-110): 21¢ per barrel on crude oil and fuel oils, $1.05 per barrel on gasoline and jet fuel, $1.68 per barrel on lubricating oils, 45% on calcined petroleum coke and 2.2¢/kg on paraffin wax. Peat (2703.00) pays 35% instead of its Column 2 rate (9903.90.08, Proclamation 10420), and steam cylinder oils (2710.19.30.50) are a Section 232 aluminum derivative at +200% (9903.85.68). The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on Russia (9903.05.66) does not apply under note 52(b). Separately, Executive Order 14066 bans imports of Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum fuels, oils and products of their distillation, LNG, coal and coal products; the calculator does not model the ban.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Russian crude, refined products, LNG and coal cannot be imported at all. Russian goods outside the ban, such as peat, pay Column 2 or in-lieu rates (35% on peat).

changes.title: No Chapter 27 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 141 Chapter 27 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no exemption for energy products. The rate is 0% in 2026. Nicaragua is a minor supplier of Chapter 27 goods.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their July 6 and August 23, 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% and 7.5% duties on Chinese Chapter 27 goods continue.

changes.title: Venezuelan oil license updated (General License 46E)
changes.detail: OFAC's current Venezuela General License 46E lets established U.S. entities (organized on or before January 29, 2025) lift, buy, refine and import Venezuelan-origin oil and petrochemical products, with payments to blocked Venezuelan government entities going into the Treasury-held Foreign Government Deposit Funds. It excludes dealings with Russian, Iranian, North Korean or Cuban persons, Chinese-controlled entities and blocked vessels. Coal is covered by General License 51D.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: energy exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect, but all 76 Chapter 27 subheadings are on the general exemption list in U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86). Crude oil, fuels, natural gas and coal from Canada, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Colombia, Guyana, Brazil, the EU and the other listed economies pay no Section 301 duty; only China still pays its older Section 301 duties.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired (energy was exempt)
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. Every Chapter 27 subheading was on its product exemption list (9903.03.03), so energy imports never paid it.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301 tariff: energy exempt
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect; all Chapter 27 subheadings, including crude oil, are on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03).

changes.title: Temporary license for Iranian oil revoked and expired
changes.detail: OFAC revoked General License X on July 7, 2026 and its wind-down license X1 expired on July 17, 2026. GL X (issued June 21, 2026) had authorized the production, delivery and sale of Iranian-origin crude oil, petrochemical and petroleum products through August 21, 2026, including importation into the United States incident to those sales. The import ban of 31 CFR 560.201 applies again in full.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) on Canadian and Mexican crude and fuels still apply.

changes.title: Russia national emergency continued; oil, LNG and coal import ban stays
changes.detail: The President continued the national emergency of Executive Order 14024, as expanded by Executive Order 14066, beyond April 15, 2026. The ban on importing Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum products, LNG and coal remains in force.

changes.title: Iranian oil already at sea temporarily allowed (General License U)
changes.detail: OFAC General License U authorized the sale, delivery and offloading — including importation into the United States — of Iranian-origin crude oil and petroleum products loaded on vessels by March 20, 2026, through April 19, 2026. It expired on that date.
changes.now: Allowed for cargoes loaded by March 20 (expired April 19, 2026)

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; energy exempt
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. All Chapter 27 subheadings were on the product exemption list (9903.03.03).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end, including the 10% on Canadian energy
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, reciprocal, Brazil, India, Venezuelan-oil, Cuba-oil and Iran tariff orders, and CBP stopped collecting the duties for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. For Chapter 27 this removed the 10% duty on non-USMCA Canadian energy, the 25% on non-USMCA Mexican goods and the 10% fentanyl duty on Chinese goods.

changes.title: India's 25% Russian-oil tariff removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) imposed because India imported Russian oil, after India committed to stop importing it. Energy products had been exempt from that duty anyway (they were on the note 2(v)(iii) exemption list).

changes.title: Tariff authorized on countries that buy from Iran
changes.detail: Executive Order 14382 allowed an additional duty (for example 25%) on goods of any country found to buy goods or services from Iran, after findings by Commerce and State. It was an IEEPA tariff and ended with Executive Order 14389 on February 24, 2026. It did not change the ban on importing Iranian goods into the United States.
changes.now: Up to +25% on a buyer country's goods (ended)

changes.title: Tariff authorized on countries that supply oil to Cuba
changes.detail: Executive Order 14380 allowed an additional duty on goods of any country found to sell or provide oil to Cuba, after findings by Commerce and State. It was an IEEPA tariff and ended with Executive Order 14389 on February 24, 2026.
changes.now: Additional duty on a supplier country's goods (ended)

changes.title: Treasury opens Venezuelan oil purchases to U.S. companies (General License 46)
changes.detail: OFAC General License 46 authorized established U.S. entities to buy, transport, refine and import Venezuelan-origin oil from the Government of Venezuela and PdVSA, with payments made into the Foreign Government Deposit Funds created by Executive Order 14373 (January 9, 2026). It has since been amended several times (46A–46E).

changes.title: Oil spill tax on imported petroleum expires; Superfund tax continues
changes.detail: The 9¢ per barrel Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund tax on imported petroleum products and domestic crude expired after December 31, 2025, (26 U.S.C. 4611(f)(2)). The petroleum Superfund tax of 16.4¢ per barrel, indexed for inflation since 2024, continues ($0.18 per barrel for 2026). These are IRS excise taxes, not customs duties, and the tariff calculator does not include them.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 cut the IEEPA duty on products of China (9903.01.24) from 20% to 10%. It applied to Chapter 27 goods, which had no energy exemption from this duty, until February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 25% tariff on India over Russian oil purchases: energy exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on products of India because India imported Russian oil. Chapter 27 products were on its exemption list (the same list as the reciprocal tariff), so Indian diesel, jet fuel and other fuels did not pay it. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Russian steam cylinder oils added to the 200% Section 232 aluminum list
changes.detail: Commerce's August 2025 inclusions put 2710.19.30.50 (steam cylinder oils) on the Section 232 aluminum derivative list (U.S. note 19(k)). Products of Russia on that list pay +200% (9903.85.68). Russian petroleum oils are banned by Executive Order 14066 in any case.

changes.title: 40% IEEPA tariff on Brazil: crude oil and fuels exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 imposed 40% on products of Brazil, but every Chapter 27 subheading, including crude oil, was on its exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada duty raised to 35%; energy stays at 10%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10); energy and energy resources (9903.01.13) stayed at 10%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: energy on the exemption list
changes.detail: The 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates applied to products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, but energy and energy products were on Annex II of Executive Order 14257, and every Chapter 27 subheading was on the exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii), 9903.01.32). Crude oil, LNG, coal and refined products never paid the reciprocal tariff. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Tariff authorized on countries that import Venezuelan oil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14245 authorized a 25% tariff, at the Secretary of State's discretion from April 2, 2025, on all goods of any country that imports Venezuelan oil. It was an IEEPA tariff and ended with Executive Order 14389 on February 24, 2026.
changes.now: Up to +25% on a buyer country's goods (ended)

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Non-USMCA Canadian energy kept paying 10% and non-USMCA Mexican goods 25%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 10% on Canadian energy, 25% on Mexican goods, 20% on Chinese goods
changes.detail: The IEEPA duties signed February 1, 2025 took effect: +10% on Canadian energy and energy resources (crude oil, natural gas, lease condensates, natural gas liquids, refined petroleum products, coal and others, 9903.01.13) and +25% on other Canadian goods (9903.01.10); +25% on goods of Mexico (9903.01.01), with no energy carve-out. China's fentanyl duty, in force since February 4, 2025 at 10%, rose to 20% (Executive Order 14228). All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 35% in place of Column 2 on certain Russian goods, including peat
changes.detail: Proclamation 10420 set a 35% rate, in place of the Column 2 rate, on listed products of Russia (9903.90.08, U.S. note 30). Peat (2703.00) is the one Chapter 27 subheading on the list.

changes.title: Russia and Belarus moved to Column 2
changes.detail: The Suspending Normal Trade Relations with Russia and Belarus Act ended normal trade relations, so products of Russia and Belarus pay Column 2 rates: 21¢ per barrel on crude oil, $1.05 per barrel on gasoline and jet fuel, 45% on calcined petroleum coke.

changes.title: Ban on Russian crude oil, petroleum products, LNG and coal
changes.detail: Executive Order 14066 prohibited the importation into the United States of Russian Federation-origin crude oil; petroleum; petroleum fuels, oils and products of their distillation; liquefied natural gas; coal; and coal products. Other forms of Russian energy are not covered (OFAC FAQ 1014). The ban is still in force and is not modeled by the tariff calculator.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of mineral fuels were **$216.4B in 2025**, -13.8% from $251.1B in 2024 and down from the 2022 peak of $322.7B, when energy prices spiked. Values move mostly with oil and gas prices, not tariffs. **Crude oil** is 68% of the total ($146.8B), refined products $49.0B, natural gas and LPG $13.1B and electricity $2.3B.

**Canada** dominates with $119.0B (55%): $90.2B of crude oil, $12.2B of natural gas and LPG, $11.3B of refined products and $2.3B of electricity. **Mexico** follows with $12.3B (down from $16.8B), then crude suppliers Saudi Arabia ($8.9B), Brazil ($6.5B), Iraq ($6.4B), Colombia ($6.4B), Guyana ($5.1B) and Nigeria ($4.6B). South Korea ($5.3B), the Netherlands ($4.0B) and India ($3.4B) ship mainly refined products.

Sanctions show clearly in the data: imports from **Russia** fell from $18.1B in 2021 to $5.3B in 2022 and to almost nothing after the March 2022 import ban, and Iran does not appear at all. **Venezuela**, whose oil sector is under U.S. sanctions, shipped $3.6B ($6.0B in 2024); since January 2026 U.S. companies can buy Venezuelan oil under OFAC General License 46. Chinese fuels, which pay Section 301 duties, were only $132M.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For energy the answer is short: **the base rate, or Free with an FTA claim, for every main supplier** — a few cents per barrel on crude oil, 52.5¢ per barrel on gasoline — and **25% extra for China**.

That is because every Chapter 27 subheading is on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies (U.S. note 52(b)), so Canada, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Brazil, Guyana, the EU, India and the others pay nothing extra. The table does **not** show sanctions: Russian crude, fuels, LNG and coal and Iranian oil cannot be imported at all, and Venezuelan oil needs a Treasury license. Nor does it include the federal petroleum and fuel excise taxes.

Excise taxes are not included: the petroleum Superfund tax ($0.18 per barrel for 2026) on imported crude and petroleum products, and 18.4¢ (gasoline) or 24.4¢ (diesel, kerosene) per gallon federal fuel tax.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 27: Mineral Fuels & Oils — Import Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Crude Oil, Fuel, LNG & Coal: EPA, DOE, CBP & Sanctions Rules and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 27) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 27 line — EPA fuel standards and renewable fuel obligations for gasoline and diesel importers, DOE natural gas import authorization, CBP petroleum gauging, Russia, Iran and Venezuela sanctions, Superfund and fuel excise taxes — and the legal ways to pay less duty: USMCA and FTA claims, petroleum substitution drawback and foreign-trade zones.

tariffEngineering.intro:
The tariff on Chapter 27 goods is small — Free to 84¢ per barrel, Free with a USMCA or FTA claim — so for most importers the bigger costs and risks are elsewhere: **sanctions** (Russian oil, LNG and coal and Iranian oil are banned; Venezuelan oil needs a Treasury license), **China's Section 301** duty of 25%, and **excise taxes** that the IRS collects on entry (the petroleum Superfund tax of 16.4¢ per barrel, indexed for inflation ($0.18 per barrel for 2026), and 18.4¢ or 24.4¢ per gallon on gasoline, diesel and kerosene).

The paperwork depends on the product: gasoline and diesel importers must meet EPA fuel-quality rules and renewable fuel obligations, natural gas and LNG imports need Department of Energy authorization, bulk petroleum is gauged and sampled by CBP, and most fuels are hazardous materials in transport. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on Canadian and Mexican crude oil and fuels
levers.saves: The base rate: 5.25–10.5¢ per barrel on crude, 52.5¢ on gasoline and jet fuel, 84¢ on lubricating oils. In 2025 a USMCA claim also avoided the 10% IEEPA duty on Canadian energy and 25% on Mexican goods.
levers.appliesTo: All dutiable lines of 2707, 2709 and 2710 for originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer (no prescribed form); claim SPI "S" on the entry. Crude oil produced in Canada or Mexico is wholly obtained there.
levers.caveat: Today a claim saves only the base rate: note 52(b) exempts Chapter 27 from the 10% Section 301 duties on Canada and Mexico with or without a claim. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim the FTA, CBTPA or AGOA rate for other suppliers
levers.saves: The per-barrel base rate on crude oil and refined products from FTA partners (Colombia, Peru, Korea, Australia, Chile, Israel, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Singapore and others), CBTPA countries such as Guyana and Trinidad and Tobago (through September 30, 2030), and AGOA countries such as Nigeria (through December 31, 2026).
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines of 2707, 2709 and 2710 whose Special column lists the program
levers.document: Origin documentation meeting the agreement's rules and the program's SPI on the entry (for example CO, R or D).
levers.caveat: GSP (A, A+) has lapsed since December 31, 2020, so a GSP code gives no benefit. A preference claim does not remove China's Section 301 duty.

citations.label: HTSUS General Notes (FTA, CBTPA note 17, AGOA)

levers.title: Use petroleum substitution drawback when you export fuels
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties (and, within limits, certain federal excise taxes) paid on imported petroleum derivatives, when a product of the same kind and quality is exported — the exported barrels do not have to be the imported ones.
levers.appliesTo: Qualified articles of headings 2707, 2708 and 2710–2715 (not crude oil of 2709)
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP under 19 U.S.C. 1313(p), matching imports to exports of the same 8-digit HTS number or commercially interchangeable product (19 CFR 191.171–191.176).
levers.caveat: Drawback of excise tax is limited to the tax paid on the substituted merchandise (19 CFR 191.171(d)). Claims must be filed within the drawback time limits.

levers.title: Store, blend or refine in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Defers duty until goods leave the zone for the U.S. market, and no duty is owed on product exported from the zone.
levers.appliesTo: Crude oil and refined products (2709, 2710) and other Chapter 27 goods handled in an approved zone or subzone
levers.document: FTZ Board authorization for the zone or subzone and CBP admission and entry procedures (15 CFR part 400; 19 CFR part 146).
levers.caveat: Zone status and any production activity (such as refining) need FTZ Board approval, which can come with conditions; admission, inventory control and entries follow CBP's zone procedures.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — China pays 25%, Russia and Iran are banned
levers.saves: 25% of value: Chinese-origin goods pay Section 301 (7.5% on a few lines); the same product from any other origin pays no extra tariff. Getting origin wrong on Russian or Iranian energy is a sanctions violation, not a duty question.
levers.appliesTo: All lines (China); crude oil, fuels, LNG and coal (Russia, Iran)
levers.document: Certificates of origin and production records showing where the oil was produced or refined. For refined products, origin follows where the goods were last substantially transformed; OFAC's guidance excludes Russian goods substantially transformed into a foreign-made product from "Russian Federation origin" (FAQ 1019). Ask CBP for a ruling when unsure.
levers.caveat: Blending or storing in a third country does not change origin. Venezuelan-origin oil may be imported only under OFAC General License 46E or a specific license.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20 (China lists)

levers.title: Claim drawback of China's Section 301 duty on re-exported goods
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the Section 301 duty paid on Chinese-origin goods that are re-exported, unused or in an exported product
levers.appliesTo: All lines, for goods of China
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Sanctions penalties and excise taxes outside the drawback rules are not refundable this way.

rules.title: Gasoline, diesel and their blendstocks: importers must register with EPA and meet the fuel quality standards (sulfur, benzene, volatility) for each imported batch, with testing by vessel, rail or truck
Gasoline and diesel importers are obligated parties under the Renewable Fuel Standard and must retire RINs for their imported volumes

rules.agency: DOE (Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management)
rules.title: Natural gas and LNG: imports require authorization from DOE under section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, applied for at least 90 days ahead
Bulk petroleum and petroleum products: CBP controls unlading and gauging (meters, shore tanks or vessel ullages) and the entry summary reports API gravity and quantity
Chemical substances and mixtures (fuels, coal-tar chemicals, waxes): TSCA import certification (positive or negative) at entry
Crude oil, gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG, LNG and flammable coal-tar products are hazardous materials in transport: shipping papers, marking and packaging
Russian Federation-origin crude oil, petroleum fuels, oils and products of their distillation, LNG, coal and coal products: import prohibited (Executive Order 14066); not in the tariff calculator
Goods of Iranian origin, including crude oil and petroleum products: import prohibited; the 2026 temporary oil licenses (GL U, GL X) have expired

citations.label: OFAC GL X and X1 (91 FR 61758)

rules.title: Venezuelan-origin oil, petrochemicals and coal from the Government of Venezuela or PdVSA: allowed for established U.S. entities under General Licenses 46E (oil) and 51D (coal), with payments into the Foreign Government Deposit Funds

Imported petroleum products (crude, refined and residual oil): petroleum Superfund excise tax of 16.4¢ per barrel, indexed for inflation ($0.18 per barrel for 2026), on entry for consumption, use or warehousing; the 9¢ oil spill tax expired after 2025 (not in the tariff calculator)

Gasoline (18.4¢ per gallon), diesel and kerosene (24.4¢ per gallon): federal excise tax on entry into the United States unless entered by bulk transfer by a registered taxable fuel registrant (then due at the terminal rack) (not in the tariff calculator)
Electricity is not entered shipment by shipment under 19 U.S.C. 1484 but on a periodic basis under Treasury regulations (Additional U.S. note 6 to Chapter 27)

groups.label: Coal and coal briquettes
groups.note: Russian-origin coal is banned (Executive Order 14066). Venezuelan coal from Carbozulia is covered by General License 51D. China pays 25% (List 3).

groups.label: Lignite
groups.note: Russian-origin lignite counts as coal under the Executive Order 14066 ban.

groups.label: Peat
groups.note: Peat is not an energy product under the Russia ban, but Russian peat pays 35% in place of the Column 2 rate.

groups.label: Coke and semicoke
groups.note: Coke is a coal product under the Russia ban. It is on no China Section 301 list.

groups.label: Coal gas and similar gases
groups.note: Manufactured gases are hazardous materials in transport.

groups.label: Coal-tar distillation products (benzene, toluene, xylenes)
groups.note: Benzene, toluene and xylenes are flammable liquids in transport. Carbazole, phenol and cresols are the only dutiable lines.

groups.label: Crude oil
groups.note: Russian and Iranian crude is banned; Venezuelan crude needs General License 46E. Every barrel also pays the petroleum Superfund excise tax ($0.18 per barrel for 2026) to the IRS.

groups.label: Refined petroleum products (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel)
groups.note: Gasoline, diesel and blendstocks fall under EPA's fuel rules and the Renewable Fuel Standard; gasoline, diesel and kerosene carry federal fuel excise tax. Lubricating oils and greases from China are on List 2 (+25%).

groups.label: Natural gas, LNG and LPG (propane, butane)
groups.note: Natural gas and LNG imports need DOE authorization. Russian-origin LNG is banned.

groups.label: Petroleum jelly and waxes
groups.note: Paraffin wax from China pays 7.5% (List 4A); the other waxes 25%.

groups.label: Petroleum coke and bitumen
groups.note: Petroleum coke and bitumen are petroleum products under the Russia ban.

groups.label: Natural bitumen, oil shale and tar sands
Electricity
groups.note: Electricity is Free from every country, including China.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about oil and gas tariffs: is there a tariff on oil from Canada, the 10% Canadian energy tariff, are oil and gas exempt, tariffs on natural gas, electricity, gasoline and diesel, Russian, Venezuelan and Iranian oil, and HS codes 2709, 2710 and 2711.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on oil, gas, coal and electricity imports — by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Base tariffs on energy are small: Free on coal, natural gas, LNG and electricity, 5.25–10.5¢ per barrel on crude oil and 52.5¢ per barrel on gasoline and jet fuel — and Free for Canada and Mexico under USMCA.

Energy is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies (U.S. note 52(b)); the 2025 IEEPA duties, including 10% on non-USMCA Canadian energy, ended February 24, 2026. Only China pays an extra tariff (25% on most lines).

Sanctions matter more than tariffs: Russian crude, fuels, LNG and coal and Iranian oil are banned, and Venezuelan oil needs an OFAC license. Federal petroleum and fuel excise taxes are owed on top; the tariff calculator includes neither.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on oil from Canada?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on oil from canada
us tariff on canadian oil and gas
faqs.answer: Only a few cents, or nothing. Canadian crude oil pays 5.25¢ per barrel (under 25° API) or 10.5¢ (25° API or more) and is Free when claimed under USMCA; refined products pay 10.5–84¢ per barrel without a claim. U.S. note 52(b) exempts all Chapter 27 goods from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada. The 10% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian energy ended on February 24, 2026. Canada supplied $119.0B of U.S. fuel imports in 2025, $90.2B of it crude oil.

faqs.question: What was the 10% tariff on Canadian energy, and is it still in effect?
searchedAs: us tariffs on canadian energy imports
does the us have tariffs on canadian energy
faqs.answer: Executive Order 14193 put an IEEPA duty on Canadian goods from March 4, 2025, at 10% for energy and energy resources (crude oil, natural gas, natural gas liquids, refined petroleum products, coal and others, heading 9903.01.13) and 25% for other goods. From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt. When the general rate rose to 35% on August 1, 2025, energy stayed at 10%. It is no longer in effect: after the Supreme Court ruled on February 20, 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, all IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are oil and gas exempt from tariffs?
searchedAs: is oil and gas exempt from tariffs
are there tariffs on crude oil
faqs.answer: From the extra tariffs, mostly yes. Every Chapter 27 subheading was on the exemption lists of the April 2025 reciprocal tariff and the 2026 Section 122 surcharge, and is on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies (U.S. note 52(b)). Base rates still apply (Free to 84¢ per barrel, Free under USMCA and most FTAs), China-origin fuels pay 25% (Section 301), and Russian and Iranian oil is banned.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. import tariff on crude oil?
faqs.answer: Crude oil (HTS 2709.00) pays 5.25¢ per barrel if it tests under 25° API (2709.00.10) and 10.5¢ per barrel at 25° API or more, including condensate (2709.00.20). It is Free from Canada and Mexico under USMCA and from FTA partners such as Colombia, and from Guyana under the CBTPA. No extra tariff applies except 25% on Chinese crude. Importers also owe the petroleum Superfund excise tax ($0.18 per barrel for 2026) to the IRS. The U.S. imported $146.8B of crude oil in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on natural gas or LNG?
searchedAs: tariff on natural gas from canada
are there tariffs on natural gas
faqs.answer: No. Natural gas by pipeline (2711.21) and LNG (2711.11) are Free from every country except China (+25%, Section 301 List 3), and are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs. Russian-origin LNG is banned. Imports need authorization from the Department of Energy (10 CFR part 590). The U.S. imported $9.6B of pipeline gas and $620M of LNG in 2025, almost all of the pipeline gas from Canada.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on electricity from Canada?
searchedAs: tariffs on electricity from canada to us
are there tariffs on electricity from canada
faqs.answer: No. Electrical energy (2716.00) is Free from every country, including China, and is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs. The 2025 IEEPA duties on Canadian goods, which exempted goods entered under USMCA, ended on February 24, 2026. Electricity is entered on a periodic basis rather than shipment by shipment (Additional U.S. note 6 to Chapter 27). The U.S. imported $2.3B of electricity in 2025, essentially all from Canada.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on imported gasoline and diesel?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on gasoline
faqs.answer: Small ones. Gasoline and jet fuel pay 52.5¢ per barrel (2710.12.15, 2710.19.16) and diesel 10.5¢ per barrel (2710.19.11), Free under USMCA and most FTAs; only Chinese fuel pays an extra 25%. The bigger costs are federal excise taxes — 18.4¢ per gallon on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel, due on entry or at the terminal rack — plus EPA fuel-quality and Renewable Fuel Standard obligations for importers.

faqs.question: Can the U.S. import Russian oil? Has the ban been lifted?
faqs.answer: No. Executive Order 14066 has banned imports of Russian-origin crude oil, petroleum fuels and products, LNG and coal since March 2022, and the President continued the underlying national emergency on March 24, 2026. On the tariff side Russia pays Column 2 rates (21¢ per barrel on crude) since April 2022. U.S. imports of Russian fuels fell from $18.1B in 2021 to almost nothing.

faqs.question: What are the oil tariffs on India?
faqs.answer: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods from August 27, 2025 because India bought Russian oil, but energy products were exempt. Executive Order 14384 removed that duty from February 7, 2026, after India committed to stop importing Russian oil. Today Indian fuels pay only the base rate: Chapter 27 is exempt from India's 10% Section 301 duty. India shipped $3.4B of fuels, mostly refined products, to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on Venezuelan oil?
searchedAs: tariffs on countries importing venezuelan oil
faqs.answer: Venezuelan crude pays only the base rate (5.25–10.5¢ per barrel); it is exempt from Venezuela's 12.5% Section 301 duty. The 2025 order allowing a 25% tariff on countries that import Venezuelan oil (Executive Order 14245) ended on February 24, 2026. Buying from the Government of Venezuela or PdVSA requires OFAC authorization: since January 29, 2026, General License 46 (now 46E) lets established U.S. companies buy and import Venezuelan oil, with payments made into Treasury-held accounts. Imports were $3.6B in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there oil tariffs on Iran or Cuba?
faqs.answer: Iranian oil cannot be imported at all: the Iran sanctions regulations ban imports of Iranian-origin goods (31 CFR 560.201). Two temporary 2026 licenses for Iranian oil (General License U, March 20 to April 19, and General License X, June 21 to July 7, wound down by July 17) have expired. Separately, 2026 executive orders allowed tariffs on countries that buy from Iran (EO 14382) or supply oil to Cuba (EO 14380); both were IEEPA tariffs and ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on oil, coal and gas from China?
faqs.answer: China-origin Chapter 27 goods pay the base rate plus 25% under Section 301 (List 3, or List 2 for lubricating oils and greases), or 7.5% for phenol, waste oils and paraffin wax (List 4A). Coke and electricity pay nothing extra. Coal from other countries is Free, and Russian coal is banned. U.S. imports from China were $132M in 2025 (down from $447M).

faqs.question: What are HS codes 2709 and 2710?
faqs.answer: 2709 is crude petroleum oil (U.S. lines 2709.00.10 under 25° API and 2709.00.20 at 25° API or more, including condensate). 2710 is refined petroleum: 2710.12 light oils (gasoline 2710.12.15, naphtha), 2710.19 other oils (diesel and fuel oils 2710.19.06/.11, jet fuel 2710.19.16, kerosene, lubricating oils 2710.19.30, greases), 2710.20 blends containing biodiesel and 2710.91/.99 waste oils.

faqs.question: What is HS code 2711?
faqs.answer: Heading 2711 covers petroleum gases: liquefied natural gas (2711.11), propane (2711.12), butanes (2711.13), ethylene, propylene, butylene and butadiene (2711.14), other liquefied gases (2711.19), natural gas in gaseous state (2711.21) and other gaseous hydrocarbons (2711.29). All are Free except from China (+25%).

faqs.question: What taxes apply to imported oil besides tariffs?
faqs.answer: Two federal excise taxes collected by the IRS, not by CBP: the petroleum Superfund tax (26 U.S.C. 4611) on crude oil and petroleum products entered for consumption, use or warehousing — 16.4¢ per barrel indexed for inflation ($0.18 per barrel for 2026); the 9¢ oil spill tax expired after 2025 — and fuel taxes of 18.4¢ per gallon on gasoline and 24.4¢ on diesel and kerosene. Neither is in the tariff calculator.
